questions.q: Meena hooks a string to a spring balance and pulls a trolley, and the pointer stops at 12 N. She writes in her notebook, 'The force on the trolley is 12 N.' What must she add so that the force is described completely?
questions.a: The direction of the pull. A force needs its direction along with its magnitude and unit, so '12 N towards the door' is complete.
o: The direction of the pull
The mass of the spring balance
The shape of the trolley top
The time for which she pulled it

questions.q: A student writes, 'The force applied by the engine is 500 Newton and its symbol is n.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: The unit's full name begins with a small letter, as in newton, because it is named after a person, while its symbol is a capital N.
o: newton for the name and N for the symbol
Newton for the name and N for the symbol
newton for the name and n for the symbol
Newton for the name and n for the symbol

questions.q: A batsman hits a ball with the same strength twice, but the first time the ball is struck towards the boundary on the off side and the second time towards the leg side. The magnitude of the force is the same. What follows from the chapter?
questions.a: The effect on the ball is different, because the effect of a force changes when its direction changes even if the magnitude stays the same.
o: The effect is different, as direction alone can change it
The effect is the same, as only magnitude decides the effect
The effect is the same, as the bat is the same both times
The effect cannot be compared without measuring the weight

questions.q: Ravi hangs a bag from a spring balance and reads 30 N. Sia holds the same balance horizontally, hooks it to a wooden block and pulls it, and reads 8 N. Which statement about the two readings is correct?
questions.a: Ravi's reading is the weight, the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the bag, while Sia's reading is the magnitude of her pull; a spring balance measures both because both are forces.
o: Both readings are forces, one being a weight and one a pull
Ravi's reading is a force but Sia's reading is a length
Ravi's reading is a mass but Sia's reading is a force
Both readings are weights since the balance only measures weight

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a complete description of a force?
questions.a: '12 N' gives only a magnitude and a unit. The other descriptions also state a direction.
o: A pull of 12 N
A push of 8 N towards the north
A weight of 5 N acting downwards
A friction of 3 N opposite to the motion

questions.q:
Read the statements about force.
Statement 1: Friction is described as acting opposite to the direction of motion.
Statement 2: The weight of an object is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls it.
Statement 3: A spring balance can measure only the weight of an object and never any other pull.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are given in the chapter. Statement 3 is false because the spring balance measures the magnitude of a force in general.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A pull of 10 N towards the east and a pull of 10 N towards the west on the same trolley do not have the same effect.
Reason (R): A force is a physical quantity for which direction has to be specified along with its magnitude.
questions.a: Both are true. The two pulls have equal magnitude but opposite direction, and the effect depends on direction too, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: True or False: 'A bag of rice has a weight of 50 N, so the weight, being a force, also has a direction.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Weight is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls the object, and a force always has a direction; here it is towards the Earth, downwards.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: weight is a force, so it has a direction (towards the Earth)

questions.q: A pupil pulls a spring balance and reads 18 N. The reading gives only the ___ of the force and not its direction.
questions.a: magnitude

questions.q:
A hockey stick hits a ball with a force of 30 N towards the east.
(a) Write the complete description of this force.
(b) The next hit is 30 N towards the north. Which part of the description has changed, and does the effect on the ball change?
questions.a: (a) 30 N towards the east (magnitude 30 N with its direction). (b) Only the direction has changed, and the effect changes because changing the direction of a force changes its effect.
s: Part (a): magnitude with unit and direction
Part (b): direction changed, so the effect changes

questions.q:
A box is pushed towards the right along a floor and the force of friction on it is 20 N.
(a) In which direction does friction act?
(b) Write the complete description of the friction force.
questions.a: (a) Friction acts opposite to the direction of the motion, that is towards the left. (b) 20 N towards the left.
s: Part (a): opposite to the motion, towards the left
Part (b): 20 N with the direction

questions.q: A ball floats at rest on water in a tub. State the direction in which the Earth's gravitational force acts on it and the direction of the buoyant force by the water, and say which is larger.
questions.a: Gravitational force acts downwards (towards the Earth) and buoyant force acts upwards. The ball is at rest, so the two are equal in magnitude.
s: Gravitational force downwards and buoyant force upwards
They are equal as the ball stays at rest

questions.q: A teacher says the spring balance in the lab is meant for weighing, yet she uses it to find how hard a student pulls a cart. Why is this allowed?
questions.a: Weight is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls an object, so it is only one kind of force. The balance measures the force with which one pulls its free end, so it gives the magnitude of any pulling force.
s: Weight is only one kind of force
Balance measures the pull on its spring, so any force's magnitude

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence correctly and state the rule behind the correction: 'The pull of the rope was 50 Newton (n).'
questions.a: The pull of the rope was 50 newton (N), or 50 N. A unit named after a person has its full name in small letters, and its symbol is capitalised.
s: Correct form: newton / N
Rule on small-letter name and capital symbol

questions.q: Nikhil says, 'A spring balance is built for weighing, so it cannot tell us the size of the pull a bullock exerts on a cart.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. A spring balance measures the magnitude of a force in general, not only weight. If one pulls its free end, it measures the force with which the spring is pulled, so it can be used for the bullock's pull as well.
s: Verdict: not correct
Balance measures the magnitude of any force
Reading gives the pull on the spring, not only weight

questions.q: Imran says, 'A ball floating on water has two forces on it, gravitational and buoyant, and to describe each completely I must give its direction too.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The gravitational force acts downwards and the buoyant force acts upwards on the floating ball. Every force is a quantity that needs direction along with its magnitude, so both descriptions must carry a direction.
s: Verdict: correct
Names the two forces with their directions
Reason: direction is needed with magnitude

questions.q: Kavya says, 'If I double the magnitude of a force, its effect changes, but if I only change its direction, the effect stays the same.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct, since changing the magnitude changes the effect. The second part is wrong: changing the direction also changes the effect, so a change in either magnitude or direction (or both) changes it.
s: Verdict: partly right
First part is correct
Second part corrected: direction also changes the effect

questions.q:
The chapter describes a ball being kicked, a ball being struck by a bat and a lemon being squeezed.
(a) Say what each force does to the object.
(b) For each, say what must be stated to describe the force completely.
(c) Which of the three shows a force changing the shape and not the motion of the object?
questions.a: (a) Kicking sets a ball at rest into motion; striking changes the direction of a moving ball; squeezing changes the shape of the lemon. (b) Each force needs its magnitude (with unit N) and its direction. (c) The squeezing of the lemon.
s: Effect of each of the three forces
Magnitude and direction needed for each
Lemon changes shape

questions.q: Prepare a short note for a Class 8 student explaining why a force is not described by its magnitude alone. Use three forces from earlier learning (friction, magnetic, gravitational) with their directions, state the unit and symbol, and say what a spring balance measures.
questions.a: Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion; like magnetic poles repel and unlike attract, so the force has a direction between the magnets; the gravitational force acts towards the Earth. The unit is the newton and its symbol is N. A spring balance measures the magnitude of a force, such as a weight or a pull.
s: Three forces with their directions
Why direction must be stated with magnitude
Unit newton and symbol N written correctly
Spring balance measures magnitude of a force

questions.q:
On sports day at a school in Pune, a group fixes a spring balance to a sledge and pulls it. Asha pulls with 18 N towards the east, Bilal pulls with 18 N towards the north on a second run, and Chitra pulls with 25 N towards the east on a third run. The readings are noted in a table.
(a) Which two runs have the same magnitude, and do they have the same effect? Give the reason.
(b) By how many newtons is Chitra's pull larger than Asha's?
(c) What does the spring balance reading tell the group and what does it not tell them?
(d) Time allows only one more run. Run X changes only the direction of Chitra's 25 N pull; run Y changes only the magnitude of Asha's pull to 30 N. Choose one and state what the group still will not learn.
questions.a: (a) Asha's and Bilal's runs; their effects are different because the directions are different. (b) 25 - 18 = 7 N. (c) It tells the magnitude of the pull but not the direction. (d) Run X shows that direction alone changes the effect but does not show what larger magnitude does; run Y shows the reverse. Either choice is accepted with the correct loss named.
s: Part (a): the two equal-magnitude runs with the reason of direction
Part (b): 7 N difference
Part (c): magnitude only, not direction
Part (d): a choice with what is left unlearnt

questions.q:
Ananya's class floats a table-tennis ball in a tub of water in a science fair at Kochi. The ball stays at rest. A visitor then gently pushes the ball to the right with a 2 N force, holding the push for a moment, and later pushes it to the left with the same 2 N force. Ananya notes that the push changes the ball's motion in both cases.
(a) Name the two forces on the ball when it floats at rest, with their directions.
(b) Which feature of the visitor's force is different in the two pushes, and what is the same?
(c) What difference in the effect should the visitor expect?
(d) Ananya can either measure the pushes with a spring balance, which gives numbers, or describe them as 'gentle' and 'firm' in words. Choose one to put in the class report and give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Gravitational force downwards and buoyant force upwards. (b) The direction differs (right, then left); the magnitude of 2 N is the same. (c) The ball is moved in opposite directions, so the effect differs. (d) Spring balance numbers are preferred because the magnitude can be measured and compared in newtons, though the direction must still be written alongside; words alone cannot be compared exactly.
s: Part (a): gravitational downwards, buoyant upwards
Part (b): direction differs, magnitude same
Part (c): effect differs because direction differs
Part (d): justified choice using measurement and direction

questions.q: In an inter-house tug of war, Red house pulls the rope to the left with 520 N and Blue house pulls it to the right with 480 N. What do the referee see and why?
questions.a: The rope moves to the left. The forces are opposite and unequal, so the net force is 520 N - 480 N = 40 N, acting towards the larger force.
o: It moves left, with a net force of 40 N
It moves right, with a net force of 40 N
It moves left, with a net force of 1000 N
It stays still, as both teams are pulling

questions.q: Two people push a stalled car in the same direction, one with 220 N and one with 180 N. A student says the net force is 40 N because 'forces always get subtracted'. What is the correct net force and the error in her reasoning?
questions.a: The net force is 400 N in the direction of the pushes. Forces in the same direction add; subtraction applies only when the forces are in opposite directions.
o: 400 N, since same-direction forces are added
40 N, since two forces are always subtracted from each other
400 N, since opposite forces are added
180 N, since the smaller force is ignored

questions.q: Which pair of forces on a block gives a non-zero net force?
questions.a: The forces of 12 N and 9 N in opposite directions are unequal, leaving 3 N in the direction of the larger one. The other pairs are equal and opposite and therefore balanced.
o: 12 N east with 9 N west
15 N right with 15 N left
8 N up with 8 N down
5 N north with 5 N south

questions.q: Two sets of forces act on identical blocks. Block P has 60 N to the right and 40 N to the left. Block Q has 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left. A student says they behave differently because the forces are very different. What does the chapter's note about net force say?
questions.a: Both have a net force of 20 N to the right, and the motion depends only on the net force, so the two blocks behave alike.
o: They behave alike, as both net forces are 20 N rightwards
P moves faster, as its individual forces are larger
Q moves faster, as its forces are smaller
They behave alike, as both net forces are 100 N rightwards

questions.q:
Read the statements about two forces along one line.
Statement 1: Two opposite forces of unequal magnitude have a net force equal to the difference of the magnitudes.
Statement 2: Two forces in the same direction have a net force equal to the difference of the magnitudes.
Statement 3: Two equal and opposite forces on a rope held by two teams leave the rope at rest.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 match the chapter. Statement 2 is false: forces in the same direction add.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tug-of-war rope moves when one team pulls with a larger force than the other.
Reason (R): A non-zero net force acts only when both teams pull in the same direction.
questions.a: A is true as unbalanced forces move the rope towards the larger force. R is false because opposite unequal forces also leave a non-zero net force.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each pair of forces on a block (column I) with the net force they produce (column II).
Column I: 1. 7 N to the right and 4 N to the left  2. 7 N to the right and 4 N to the right  3. 9 N to the left and 9 N to the right  4. 4 N to the left and 11 N to the right
Column II: a. Zero  b. 3 N to the right  c. 11 N to the right  d. 7 N to the right
questions.a: In 1 the opposite forces leave 7 - 4 = 3 N to the right; in 2 they add to 11 N right; in 3 they cancel to zero; in 4 they leave 11 - 4 = 7 N to the right.

questions.q: True or False: 'When two forces act on an object, the magnitude of the net force is always the difference of the two magnitudes.' Give the verdict and a reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The net force is the difference only when the forces are opposite; when they act in the same direction it is the sum of the magnitudes.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: sum for same direction, difference for opposite

questions.q:
Two people push a stalled car in the same direction with 300 N and 250 N.
(a) What is the net force?
(b) The person pushing with 250 N turns round and pushes the other way by mistake. What are the net force and its direction now?
questions.a: (a) 300 N + 250 N = 550 N in the direction of the pushes. (b) 300 N - 250 N = 50 N in the direction of the 300 N push.
s: Part (a): 550 N forward
Part (b): 50 N towards the larger force

questions.q: Two teams pull a rope with 400 N each in opposite directions. State what such forces are called, and the net force and the state of the rope.
questions.a: They are balanced forces. The net force is zero, so the rope does not move.
s: Called balanced forces
Net force is zero and the rope does not move

questions.q:
In an arm-wrestling match, player R pushes with 80 N and player S pushes in the opposite direction with 65 N.
(a) Find the net force on the joined hands.
(b) Towards whom do the hands tilt?
questions.a: (a) 80 N - 65 N = 15 N. (b) The hands tilt towards S, along the larger force of R, so S's arm is pushed back.
s: Part (a): 15 N
Part (b): direction of the larger force, towards S

questions.q: Differentiate between balanced and unbalanced forces by their net force and by what happens to a rope in a tug of war, with an example of each.
questions.a: Balanced forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero and the rope does not move, as when both teams pull with 400 N. Unbalanced forces leave a non-zero net force and the rope moves towards the larger force, as with 450 N against 400 N.
s: Balanced: net force zero, rope stays, example
Unbalanced: non-zero net force, rope moves, example

questions.q:
A block feels 60 N to the right and 40 N to the left in one trial, and 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left in another.
(a) Find the net force in each trial.
(b) Will the block move differently in the two trials? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Both trials: 60 - 40 = 20 N and 30 - 10 = 20 N to the right. (b) No, because the motion depends only on the net force, which is the same.
s: Part (a): 20 N to the right in each trial
Part (b): same net force, so same motion

questions.q: Zoya says, 'In a tug of war, if team A pulls with 350 N and team B with 300 N, the rope stays at rest because both teams are pulling.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The forces are opposite but unequal, so they are unbalanced. The net force is 350 N - 300 N = 50 N towards team A, and the rope moves in that direction.
s: Verdict: not correct
Net force 50 N from the difference
Rope moves towards the larger force

questions.q: Dev says, 'Two students pushing a stalled car in the same direction with 120 N and 90 N give a net force of 210 N in that direction.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. For forces in the same direction the net force is the sum of the magnitudes, 120 N + 90 N = 210 N, and its direction is the direction of the pushes.
s: Verdict: correct
Sum 210 N for same-direction forces
Direction is that of the pushes

questions.q: Write one situation for a block in which two forces give a net force of 4 N to the left, and one in which two forces give a net force of zero. Give the numbers.
questions.a: E.g. 10 N to the left and 6 N to the right give 10 - 6 = 4 N to the left; 9 N to the left and 9 N to the right are balanced and give zero net force.
s: Situation with a 4 N net force to the left, with numbers
Situation with zero net force, with numbers
Directions of the forces consistent with the net force

questions.q: Two forces of 14 N and 9 N act on a block on a table in three arrangements. In (a) both act to the right. In (b) 14 N acts to the right and 9 N to the left. In (c) 14 N acts to the left and 9 N to the right. Find the magnitude and direction of the net force in each, and state the rule used for same-direction and for opposite forces.
questions.a: (a) 14 + 9 = 23 N to the right. (b) 14 - 9 = 5 N to the right. (c) 14 - 9 = 5 N to the left. Same direction: add. Opposite: subtract and take the direction of the larger force.
s: Net force in (a)
Net force in (b) with direction
Net force in (c) with direction
Rule for same-direction forces
Rule for opposite forces

questions.q: In a school tug of war, team X pulls with 640 N and team Y with 640 N, and the rope does not move. After ten seconds team Y tires and pulls with 590 N. Describe the rope in each stage, give the net force and its direction, name the type of forces, and say how much more Y must pull to restore the first stage.
questions.a: First stage: equal and opposite, balanced forces, net force zero, rope at rest. Second stage: unbalanced, net force 640 - 590 = 50 N towards X, so the rope moves towards X. Y must pull 50 N more to return to 640 N.
s: First stage: balanced and zero net force
Rope at rest in the first stage
Second stage: unbalanced forces and net force 50 N
Rope moves towards the larger force, team X
Y needs 50 N more

questions.q:
Red and Blue houses meet in the final tug of war at a school in Hyderabad. In round 1, Red pulls with 520 N and Blue with 480 N. For round 2, Blue adds a student who adds 60 N to Blue's pull, and Red's pull stays at 520 N. Before round 3 Red's coach can add either Arun, who adds 35 N, or Bhavna, who adds 20 N, to Red's pull.
(a) Find the net force and its direction in round 1.
(b) Find the net force and its direction in round 2.
(c) With Arun in round 3, what is the net force and who wins the pull? What happens with Bhavna?
(d) Arun tires after one pull but Bhavna stays steady; the match is a best of three. Choose one for round 3 and say what Red gives up.
questions.a: (a) 520 - 480 = 40 N towards Red. (b) Blue's pull is 540 N, so 540 - 520 = 20 N towards Blue. (c) With Arun Red pulls 555 N against 540 N, a net force of 15 N towards Red; with Bhavna Red pulls 540 N, equal to Blue, so the forces are balanced and the rope does not move. (d) Arun gives Red a win in round 3 but the gain may vanish later, while Bhavna gives a steady draw; either choice is accepted if the loss is named.
s: Part (a): 40 N towards Red
Part (b): 20 N towards Blue
Part (c): 15 N towards Red with Arun, balanced with Bhavna
Part (d): a choice with what Red gives up

questions.q:
A car stalls on a road in Nashik. Two passers-by push it forward with 180 N and 140 N. The road and the air together oppose the motion with a total force of 300 N. The car starts to move only when the net force on it is in the forward direction. A third passer-by can either push with a force of 45 N, or two children can push together with 25 N each.
(a) What is the combined force of the first two pushes?
(b) What is the net force on the car once the opposing 300 N is included, and does it begin to move?
(c) Find the net force with the third passer-by, and with the two children.
(d) The two children need time to reach the car, while the adult is already there. Choose one and say what you lose.
questions.a: (a) 180 + 140 = 320 N forward. (b) 320 - 300 = 20 N forward, so the car begins to move. (c) With the adult 20 + 45 = 65 N; with the two children 20 + 25 + 25 = 70 N. (d) The adult acts at once but adds 5 N less in net force; the children give 5 N more net force but only after a delay. Either choice is accepted with the loss named.
s: Part (a): 320 N forward
Part (b): 20 N forward and the car moves
Part (c): 65 N and 70 N
Part (d): a choice with the loss named

questions.q: A rope is pulled with 410 N by one team and with 375 N by the other team in the opposite direction. The net force on the rope, in newtons, is ___.
A shopkeeper pushes a heavy carton with 40 N and it does not move; the largest friction the floor can offer is 50 N. Which statement is right?
questions.a: The carton starts moving only when the push is larger than the force of friction; 40 N is not larger than 50 N, so the push is not enough and the net force on the carton is zero.
o: Push not above friction, so net force is zero
The push is larger than friction, so the carton moves slowly
There is no friction yet, as the carton is not moving
The friction is 40 N, which is larger than the 50 N push

questions.q: A stack of coins is released from a stretched rubber band on four surfaces with the same stretch. It travels 20 cm on the cement floor, 35 cm on the wooden table, 52 cm on the laminated table and 70 cm on the marble floor. On which surface is the friction the second largest?
questions.a: The distance is smaller where friction is larger, so the cement floor has the largest friction and the wooden table the second largest.
o: The wooden table
The cement floor
The laminated table
The marble floor

questions.q: A stack of coins slides 40 cm after leaving the rubber band, and Rhea says the rubber band is still pushing it along. What is the right correction?
questions.a: Once contact with the rubber band is lost, its force no longer acts; only the force of friction acts, opposite to the motion, and it reduces the velocity until the stack stops.
o: Only friction acts now, opposite to the motion, and slows it
Only the rubber band acts now, along the motion, and speeds it
Friction and the rubber band both act, balancing each other
No force acts now, so the stack keeps its velocity for ever

questions.q: A box is being pushed along a floor. Which of the following is NOT one of the forces listed for the box in the chapter?
questions.a: A 'force of motion' that stays after the push stops is not among the listed forces. The applied force, friction, weight and the normal force are.
o: A force of motion that remains once the push stops
The force of friction from the floor on the box
The weight acting downwards on the box
The normal force from the floor, acting upwards on it

questions.q:
Read the statements about friction.
Statement 1: For the same stretch of the rubber band, the force of friction is the same on every surface.
Statement 2: On a box being pushed, the weight and the normal force are balanced.
Statement 3: The spring-balance reading at the point the block just starts to move gives an approximate measure of the force of friction.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: the stack travels different distances on different surfaces, so friction differs with the surface.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cyclist who stops pedalling on a level road comes to rest after travelling some distance.
Reason (R): The force of friction acts on the bicycle in the direction opposite to its motion.
questions.a: Both are true. Friction opposes the motion and reduces the velocity gradually, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
The same stretched rubber band launches a stack of coins on four surfaces. Match each surface with the distance travelled (column I) to the rank of its friction (column II).
Column I: 1. Surface P, 52 cm  2. Surface Q, 18 cm  3. Surface R, 35 cm  4. Surface S, 70 cm
Column II: a. Greatest friction  b. Least friction  c. Second least friction  d. Second greatest friction
questions.a: The shorter the distance, the greater the friction. Q (18 cm) is greatest, R (35 cm) second greatest, P (52 cm) second least and S (70 cm) least.

questions.q: A block just starts to move when the spring balance reads 7 N on one surface and 4.5 N on another. The first surface has about ___ N more friction than the second.

The stretched rubber band is released and the stack of coins starts moving.
(a) Why does it start moving?
(b) Which force acts on it after it loses contact with the rubber band, and what is its effect?
questions.a: (a) The force of the rubber band is larger than the force of friction, so a net force acts forward and gives it acceleration. (b) Only the force of friction acts, opposite to the motion, and it gradually decreases the velocity until the stack stops.
s: Part (a): rubber band force larger than friction, net force forward
Part (b): friction alone, slows the stack to rest

questions.q:
A wooden block is pulled with a spring balance and just begins to move when the reading is 9 N.
(a) What does this reading indicate?
(b) The block then moves at constant velocity under a steady pull. What is the net force on it, and what does that say about the friction?
questions.a: (a) It gives an approximate measure of the force of friction, about 9 N. (b) The net force is zero because the velocity is neither increasing nor decreasing, so the friction balances the pull.
s: Part (a): about 9 N, friction
Part (b): net force zero, friction balances the pull

questions.q: Why does a bicycle come to rest some distance after the rider stops pedalling, and what must the rider do to keep it moving at the same speed?
questions.a: Friction acts opposite to the motion and brings the bicycle to rest. To keep it moving the rider must keep applying a force that counters the force of friction.
s: Friction against the motion stops the bicycle
Continuous force needed to counter friction

questions.q:
A carton of weight 200 N is pushed along a level floor.
(a) Name the two vertical forces on it, with their directions.
(b) How do their magnitudes compare, and what is the normal force?
questions.a: (a) The weight (gravitational force) acts downwards and the normal force acts upwards, perpendicular to the surface. (b) They are balanced, so the normal force is also 200 N.
s: Part (a): weight down, normal force up
Part (b): balanced, normal force 200 N

questions.q: Compare the stack of coins on marble and on a wooden table with the same stretch of the rubber band, in terms of the friction, the way the velocity falls and the distance travelled.
questions.a: On marble the friction is smaller, so the velocity falls more slowly and the stack travels farther. On the wooden table the friction is larger, so the velocity falls faster and the stack stops sooner.
s: Friction smaller on marble, larger on wood
Slower fall in velocity and larger distance on marble

questions.q: Arti says, 'Friction acts in the same direction as the motion, so a rougher floor should make the coins travel farther.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. Friction acts in the direction opposite to the motion, and a rougher surface gives more friction, so the velocity falls faster and the coins travel a smaller distance.
s: Verdict: not correct
Friction is opposite to the motion
Rougher surface means more friction and a shorter distance

questions.q: Karan says, 'If the spring-balance reading at the start of motion is 8 N on one surface and 6 N on another, the coins will travel a smaller distance on the 8 N surface.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. A larger reading means a larger force of friction, and with larger friction the velocity decreases faster, so the coins travel a smaller distance on the 8 N surface.
s: Verdict: correct
Larger reading means larger friction
Larger friction, smaller distance

questions.q: Mohan says, 'Air also exerts a force of friction on a moving box, but it is always exactly zero.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Air does exert a force of friction on a box moving through it, so it is not truly zero. In many cases its magnitude is so small that it can be neglected, which is different from being exactly zero.
s: Verdict: partly right
Air does exert friction
It is small enough to neglect in many cases, not always zero

questions.q: In Activity 6.1 a stack of coins is released by the same stretched rubber band on a wooden table, a laminated table and a polished marble floor, and it stops after 30 cm, 45 cm and 75 cm in that order. Explain the motion of the stack from release to rest in terms of forces, compare the friction on the three surfaces and give the conclusion.
questions.a: Before release the forces are balanced. On release the rubber band's force is larger than friction, so a net force acts forward and the stack accelerates. After losing contact only friction acts, opposite to the motion, and slows it to rest. The distance rises from wood to laminate to marble, so friction is largest on the wooden table and smallest on marble: it depends on the nature of the surfaces.
s: Forces balanced before release
Net force forward at release gives acceleration
Only friction after contact is lost, stack slows and stops
Ordering of friction on the three surfaces
Conclusion: friction depends on the nature of the surfaces

questions.q: Four surfaces are tested with the spring balance of Activity 6.2, and the reading when the block just starts to move is 6 N on wood, 4 N on laminate, 2 N on marble and 9 N on cement. Rank the surfaces by friction, predict the order of distances travelled by the stack of coins, say by how much cement exceeds marble, and explain why the reading is only an approximate measure of friction.
questions.a: Ranking from largest friction: cement (9 N), wood (6 N), laminate (4 N), marble (2 N). The distances travelled run in the reverse order: marble farthest, then laminate, wood and cement shortest. Cement exceeds marble by 9 - 2 = 7 N. The reading is approximate because it is taken at the point the block just starts to move, when the pull is only about equal to friction.
s: Ranking by friction
Predicted order of distances reversed
7 N difference
Link between the reading and the friction
Reading approximate: taken as the block just starts to move

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur wants to choose a floor for a new corridor. A student carries out Activity 6.2 with a wooden block and records the spring-balance reading at the instant the block just starts to move: 6 N on the wooden floor, 4 N on laminate, 2 N on polished marble and 9 N on cement. She also releases a stack of coins with the same stretched rubber band on each surface.
(a) Which surface will give the stack its greatest travel and which its least?
(b) By how much does the friction on cement exceed that on marble?
(c) What does a smaller reading say about how the velocity of the coins falls?
(d) The corridor is used by children who walk and run and also by trolleys carrying books. Choose marble or cement for it and give a reason from the chapter, saying what the choice costs.
questions.a: (a) Greatest travel on marble and least on cement. (b) 9 N - 2 N = 7 N. (c) A smaller reading means smaller friction, so the velocity falls more slowly. (d) Cement is chosen for walking since friction helps feet grip and prevents slipping, but trolleys are harder to move; marble makes trolleys glide easily but walking on polished floors is more risky. Either choice is accepted with the cost named.
s: Part (a): marble greatest, cement least
Part (b): 7 N
Part (c): slower fall of velocity
Part (d): a choice with a reason and the cost

questions.q:
A carton weighing 200 N is on the floor of a godown in Surat. A worker pushes it horizontally, and the largest force of friction the floor can offer against its motion is 80 N. He pushes first with 50 N, then with 80 N, then with 95 N. A second worker suggests moving the carton to a polished corridor, where the largest friction is only 30 N.
(a) What happens at 50 N, and what is the force of friction then?
(b) What are the two vertical forces on the carton and their values?
(c) What is the net force at 95 N and its direction?
(d) In the corridor the carton keeps sliding for some distance after each push, and it may hit a wall. Choose the godown floor or the corridor and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) The carton does not move because 50 N is not larger than the friction, which balances the push. (b) The weight, 200 N downwards, and the normal force, 200 N upwards, balanced. (c) 95 - 80 = 15 N in the direction of the push. (d) The godown floor is steadier and the carton stops soon, but it needs a bigger push; the corridor needs only a small push but the carton keeps sliding after the push. Either choice with the cost named is accepted.
s: Part (a): no motion at 50 N since the push does not exceed friction
Part (b): weight and normal force each 200 N, opposite
Part (c): 15 N forward
Part (d): a choice with what is given up

questions.q: A porter at a railway station pushes a trolley along a straight level platform. It moves at a constant velocity while he pushes with 18 N. What is the force of friction on the trolley?
questions.a: The velocity is constant, so the net force is zero and the friction must be equal to the push, 18 N, acting in the opposite direction.
o: 18 N, opposite to the push
18 N, in the direction of the push
0 N, since the trolley is moving
Less than 18 N, since it is moving

questions.q: A bus travels around a roundabout at a steady speed of 30 km per hour. A student says there is no net force because the speed does not change. What is the correct reasoning?
questions.a: Constant velocity means no change in magnitude or direction. The direction changes on a curve, so the velocity changes, the acceleration is not zero and a net force acts.
o: Direction changes, so velocity changes and a net force acts
Speed is constant, so the velocity is constant and the net force is zero
Direction changes only matter when the speed changes as well
Net force is zero whenever the speed of the bus is fixed

questions.q: On a smooth ice surface a puck moves in a straight line at 4 m/s. If friction and air are neglected and no other force acts, what does the puck do?
questions.a: With zero net force, an object in motion continues with the same constant velocity, so it keeps moving at 4 m/s in a straight line.
o: It moves on at 4 m/s in the same direction
It slows down and stops after a short time
It speeds up steadily as it keeps moving
It turns slowly towards the side it was pushed

questions.q: When no net force acts on an object, which of the following is NOT possible?
questions.a: With zero net force the acceleration is zero, so the object cannot be moving with a constant acceleration. It can be at rest or moving with constant velocity.
o: It is moving with a constant acceleration
It remains at rest if it was at rest
It keeps a constant velocity if it was moving
It has zero acceleration at every instant

questions.q:
Read the statements on the first law.
Statement 1: If the net force on an object is zero, its acceleration is zero.
Statement 2: A body moving at constant velocity needs a continuing net force in its direction to keep moving.
Statement 3: Galileo argued that a body on a horizontal plane would move indefinitely if all impediments were removed.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are given in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: no net force is needed to keep an object moving with constant velocity.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A box pushed with 30 N on a floor that gives a friction of 30 N will slow down and stop.
Reason (R): When the net force on an object is zero, its acceleration is zero.
questions.a: A is false: the forces are balanced, so the box continues with constant velocity. R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: True or False: 'A cart moves along a level track at a constant 2 m/s, so a net force must be acting on it in the direction of its motion.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. A constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero; any push along the motion is balanced by friction.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: zero net force for constant velocity

questions.q: A skater glides in a straight line at 6 m/s with zero net force on her. Her velocity after 10 s is ___ m/s.

An object has no net force acting on it.
(a) What are the two possible states of the object?
(b) Describe the shape of its velocity-time graph in each.
questions.a: (a) It is either at rest or moving with constant velocity. (b) For rest, the velocity-time graph is a straight line along the time axis at zero velocity; for constant velocity, it is a straight line parallel to the time axis at that velocity.
s: Part (a): at rest or constant velocity
Part (b): a horizontal line at zero or at the constant value

questions.q: If no net force acts on an object, which of these are possible: (i) it stays at rest if at rest, (ii) it keeps moving with constant velocity if moving, (iii) it moves with constant acceleration? Give the reason for the one that is not.
questions.a: (i) and (ii) are possible. (iii) is not, because zero net force means zero acceleration.
s: (i) and (ii) possible
(iii) impossible since zero net force gives zero acceleration

questions.q: A car moves at a constant velocity. State what this tells you about its speed and about its direction, with a one-line example of motion that does not have a constant velocity even though the speed is steady.
questions.a: Both the magnitude and the direction of the velocity stay unchanged, so the car moves in a straight line at a steady speed. Moving round a bend at a steady speed is not constant velocity as the direction changes.
s: Magnitude and direction unchanged
Example of steady speed but changing direction

questions.q:
A person pushes a moving box forward with 45 N and the force of friction is 45 N.
(a) What does the box do?
(b) What happens if she stops pushing, and why?
questions.a: (a) The forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero and the box continues to move with constant velocity. (b) Only the friction then acts opposite to the motion, so the box slows down and stops.
s: Part (a): constant velocity, since net force is zero
Part (b): only friction acts, so it slows to rest

questions.q: What is inertia, and how did Galileo's idea of removing all impediments to motion differ from the earlier belief about moving objects?
questions.a: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Earlier it was thought that a force was needed to keep an object moving at constant velocity; Galileo argued it would continue indefinitely if all impediments were removed.
s: Inertia as resisting a change in state
Earlier belief versus Galileo's argument

questions.q: A position-time graph for an object is a straight horizontal line at 8 m from 0 s to 10 s. What is the velocity of the object, and is a net force acting on it?
questions.a: The position does not change, so the velocity is zero. The object is at rest and no net force acts on it.
s: Velocity is zero
No net force as the object stays at rest

questions.q: Meena says, 'A ball rolling on a level floor comes to rest, which proves that a force is needed to keep an object moving.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The ball stops because the force of friction acts opposite to its motion, producing a net force. With no net force the ball would continue at constant velocity, so no force is needed to keep it moving.
s: Verdict: not correct
Friction is the force that stops the ball
Without net force the velocity stays constant

questions.q: Sandeep says, 'An object moving at 5 m/s in a straight line with no net force has a position-time graph that is a horizontal straight line.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. A horizontal line means the position does not change, which is the object at rest. At 5 m/s the position grows by 5 m every second, so the graph is a straight line sloping upwards.
s: Verdict: not correct
Horizontal line means rest
Constant velocity gives a sloping straight line

questions.q: Sunita says, 'With no friction, a net force is needed to set an object at rest moving, and a continuing net force is needed to keep it moving at constant velocity.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Without friction a net force is needed to set an object at rest in motion. But once it moves, no further force is needed to keep it moving at constant velocity; a force is needed only to change its velocity or stop it.
s: Verdict: partly right
First part correct
Second part corrected

questions.q: Explain with Newton's first law the motion of a box in these three cases: (a) a box at rest on a floor with no net force, (b) a box pushed forward with a force equal to the friction on it, (c) the same box when the person stops pushing. Describe the net force and the velocity-time graph in (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Net force zero, so the box stays at rest; the velocity-time graph is a line at zero. (b) Applied force and friction are equal and opposite, net force zero, so the box continues with constant velocity; the graph is a line parallel to the time axis. (c) Only friction acts, a net force opposite to the motion, so the velocity decreases and the box stops.
s: Net force zero and rest in (a)
Graph for (a)
Balanced forces and constant velocity in (b)
Graph for (b)
Only friction in (c), slowing to rest

questions.q: Do the thought experiment of the chapter: the stack of coins is released by the stretched rubber band on an imagined floor with zero friction. Predict the motion, name the law that explains it, say how it differs from the real surfaces, and state what would be needed to stop it or to change its direction.
questions.a: The stack would keep moving with the same constant velocity for ever, since the net force is zero. This follows from Newton's first law. On real surfaces friction slows the stack to rest. To stop it or to change its velocity (magnitude or direction) a force would have to be applied.
s: Prediction of constant velocity for ever
Newton's first law named
Contrast with real surfaces having friction
A force needed to stop it
A force also needed to change its direction

questions.q:
At Chennai airport a trolley loaded with bags is pushed along a straight, level corridor. The porter pushes with 30 N and the trolley moves at a constant velocity of 1.5 m/s for 40 s. The friction on the trolley is the only other horizontal force.
(a) What is the friction on the trolley, and what is the net force?
(b) How far does the trolley move in 40 s?
(c) The porter stops pushing 10 m before the end of the corridor. Describe what happens to the trolley and why.
(d) The porter can either keep pushing at 30 N all the way, or stop pushing earlier and let the trolley coast. Choose one and say what you lose.
questions.a: (a) Friction is 30 N opposite to the push and the net force is zero. (b) 1.5 m/s x 40 s = 60 m. (c) Only friction acts, opposite to the motion, so the velocity falls and the trolley slows and may stop before the end. (d) Pushing all the way keeps the arrival time but costs effort; coasting saves effort but the trolley slows, takes longer and may stop short. Either choice is accepted with the loss named.
s: Part (a): 30 N friction and zero net force
Part (b): 60 m
Part (c): friction alone slows it
Part (d): a choice with what is lost

questions.q:
In a school lab, two objects P and Q are observed for 6 s with no net force on either. The position-time graph of P is a straight horizontal line at 8 m. The graph of Q is a straight line sloping upwards from 0 m at 0 s to 30 m at 6 s.
(a) What is the velocity of P and of Q?
(b) What is the net force on each, and why?
(c) Describe the velocity-time graph of each.
(d) A teacher must show the first law to Class 7 in one demonstration, either with a body at rest like P or with a body moving at constant velocity like Q on a real table with friction. Choose one and say what the audience may miss.
questions.a: (a) P: 0 m/s; Q: 30 m / 6 s = 5 m/s. (b) Both have zero net force, because one is at rest and the other moves with constant velocity. (c) P: a line along the time axis at zero; Q: a line parallel to the time axis at 5 m/s. (d) The rest demonstration is simple and shows no net force clearly; the Q demonstration shows more but needs a push equal to friction, which may confuse. Either choice is accepted with the loss named.
s: Part (a): 0 and 5 m/s
Part (b): zero net force for both
Part (c): horizontal lines at 0 and at 5 m/s
Part (d): a choice with what is missed

questions.q: A crate is pulled along a level floor at a constant velocity with a rope. The rope is then cut. Ignoring air, what is the best description of what the crate does next?
questions.a: After the rope is cut only friction acts, opposite to the motion, so a net force opposes the motion and the crate slows down until it stops.
o: It slows to a stop, as friction has no balancing pull
It keeps going at the same velocity, as no force acts on it at all
It speeds up for a moment, then slows down as friction acts
It stops at once, because motion always needs a continuing pull

questions.q: A net force of 24 N acts on a cart of 8 kg and then the same net force acts on a cart of 12 kg. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: a = F/m gives 3 m/s2 for the 8 kg cart and 2 m/s2 for the 12 kg cart; for the same force the larger mass has the smaller acceleration.
o: The 8 kg cart accelerates at 3 m/s2, the 12 kg cart at 2 m/s2
The 8 kg cart accelerates at 2 m/s2, the 12 kg cart at 3 m/s2

The 8 kg cart accelerates at 192 m/s2, the 12 kg cart at 288 m/s2

questions.q: A student of mass 45 kg stands still on a weighing scale in a lift hall. Using g = 9.8 m/s2, her weight, the gravitational force on her, is closest to which value?
questions.a: F = mg = 45 kg x 9.8 m/s2 = 441 N, directed downwards towards the Earth.

questions.q: Two stones of 1 kg and 5 kg are dropped together from the same height near the Earth's surface. A student says the 5 kg stone has the larger acceleration because its weight is larger. What does the chapter say?
questions.a: Weight is 5 times larger but so is the mass, so a = F/m = g for both. The acceleration due to gravity does not depend on the mass of the object.
o: Both fall with equal acceleration g, whatever the mass
The 5 kg stone has 5 times the acceleration of the 1 kg stone
The 1 kg stone has 5 times the acceleration of the 5 kg stone
Both have zero acceleration since their weights are balanced

questions.q: A cricketer catches a fast ball and at once draws his hands back with the ball. Why does this reduce the hurt to his hands?
questions.a: It makes the ball's velocity fall to zero over a longer time, so its acceleration is smaller, and hence the force the ball and hands exert on each other is smaller.
o: Longer stopping time gives smaller acceleration and force
The time of stopping is shorter, so the force on the hands is smaller
The ball loses its mass while being drawn back with the hands
The velocity of the ball stays the same, so no force acts

questions.q: A coconut dropped on a hard concrete floor breaks, but the same coconut dropped onto a thick pile of hay does not. Which is the best explanation?
questions.a: On the hard floor the coconut stops in a very short time, so the acceleration and the force on it are very large and break the shell; the hay lengthens the time of stopping, which reduces the force.
o: The hay lengthens the stopping time, so the force is smaller
The hay reduces the mass of the coconut, so the shell is stronger
The hay increases the weight of the coconut, which protects the shell
The floor pulls the coconut with a force that hay removes

questions.q:
Read the statements about the second law.
Statement 1: One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s2.
Statement 2: The acceleration of an object has the same direction as the net force on it.
Statement 3: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface does not depend on the mass of the falling object.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are in the chapter: the definition of newton, the direction of acceleration along the net force, and the independence of g from mass.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 2 kg object and a 10 kg object dropped near the Earth's surface have the same acceleration.
Reason (R): The weight of the 10 kg object is larger than the weight of the 2 kg object.
questions.a: Both are true. The larger weight is true but it is not why the accelerations are equal; the acceleration F/m = g is the same since the force and the mass increase in the same proportion.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with the acceleration produced (column II).
Column I: 1. Net force 60 N on a 12 kg object  2. Net force 90 N on a 30 kg object  3. Net force 45 N on a 5 kg object  4. Net force 48 N on an 8 kg object
Column II: a. 3 m/s2  b. 5 m/s2  c. 6 m/s2  d. 9 m/s2
For a quick estimate with g = 10 m/s2, a bag of mass 7.5 kg has a weight of ___ N.

A student pushes a stationary 40 kg block with a force that exceeds the maximum friction of 48 N by 12 N, that is with 60 N.

(b) Find the displacement in 4 s from rest.
s: Part (a): 0.3 m/s2
Part (b): 2.4 m

questions.q:
A motor-cycle with its rider has a total mass of 300 kg and the net force on it is 600 N.
(a) Find its acceleration.
(b) A pillion rider of mass 100 kg joins, and the net force stays at 600 N. Find the new acceleration.
questions.a: (a) 600/300 = 2 m/s2. (b) 600/(300 + 100) = 1.5 m/s2, smaller since the mass is larger.
s: Part (a): 2 m/s2
Part (b): 1.5 m/s2

questions.q:
Two stones of 1 kg and 5 kg are dropped near the Earth's surface (g = 9.8 m/s2).
(a) State the acceleration of each.
(b) Find the gravitational force on each.
questions.a: (a) Both have an acceleration of 9.8 m/s2. (b) 1 x 9.8 = 9.8 N and 5 x 9.8 = 49 N.
s: Part (a): same acceleration 9.8 m/s2
Part (b): 9.8 N and 49 N

questions.q: Explain with the second law why airbags in cars reduce injury in a collision.
questions.a: The airbag inflates into a soft cushion, so the head and chest take a longer time to come to rest. The same change in velocity in a longer time means a smaller acceleration, so the force on the person is smaller.
s: Longer time of stopping
Smaller acceleration and so smaller force

questions.q: A coconut is brought down at a high velocity and cracks on hitting hard ground. Explain with F = ma why the shell breaks.
questions.a: The coconut stops in a very short time, so its velocity changes very quickly and its acceleration is very large. The ground must exert a very large force, and that force breaks the shell.
s: Very short stopping time gives large acceleration
Large force from the ground breaks the shell

questions.q: Rohit says, 'A 10 kg object falls with a larger acceleration than a 2 kg object because its weight is larger.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The weight is larger, but so is the mass. a = F/m = mg/m = g, the same for both, because g does not depend on the mass of the object.
s: Verdict: not correct
Weight divided by mass gives g
g does not depend on mass

questions.q: Neha says, 'If I double the force on a trolley and also double its mass, the acceleration doubles.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. Doubling the force doubles a, doubling the mass halves it; so a = 2F/2m = F/m, which is unchanged.
s: Verdict: not correct
Doubling the force doubles the acceleration
Doubling the mass halves it, so there is no net change

questions.q: Pooja says, 'One newton gives 1 m/s2 to a 1 kg mass, so a 3 kg mass needs 3 N to get the same acceleration of 1 m/s2.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. F = ma = 3 kg x 1 m/s2 = 3 N, so the force needed for the same acceleration increases in proportion to the mass.
s: Verdict: correct
Applies F = ma with the numbers
Force proportional to mass at fixed acceleration

questions.q: Show that a net force of 20 N cannot give a 4 kg block an acceleration of 8 m/s2. State what acceleration it does give and what force is needed for 8 m/s2.
questions.a: F = ma needs 4 x 8 = 32 N for 8 m/s2, not 20 N. The 20 N force gives 20/4 = 5 m/s2.
s: Force needed is 32 N, more than 20 N
Acceleration with 20 N is 5 m/s2
Conclusion: 8 m/s2 is not possible with 20 N

questions.q: A car of mass 800 kg moving east has a velocity-time graph that rises in a straight line from 0 to 12 m/s in the first 4 s, stays flat at 12 m/s for the next 6 s, and falls in a straight line to 0 in the next 4 s. Find the force on the car in each of the three intervals with its direction, and the total distance travelled.
questions.a: 0-4 s: a = 12/4 = 3 m/s2, F = 800 x 3 = 2400 N east. 4-10 s: constant velocity, force zero. 10-14 s: a = -12/4 = -3 m/s2, F = -2400 N, that is 2400 N towards the west. Distance = 24 m + 72 m + 24 m = 120 m.
s: Force 2400 N east in the first interval
Zero force in the flat interval
2400 N towards the west while slowing
Distance in each interval
Total 120 m

questions.q: In Activity 6.3 a cart starts from rest and covers the same distance in time T1 = 2.0 s with one cup load, and in T2 = 1.6 s when the load in the cup is doubled. Use s = 1/2 aT squared to find a2/a1, compare with the expected value, and explain the difference.
questions.a: Equal distances give a1T1 squared = a2T2 squared, so a2/a1 = (T1/T2) squared = (2.0/1.6) squared = 1.5625. Doubling the force should double the acceleration, so 2 is expected. The measured ratio is a little less than 2 because of friction between the wheels and the surface and measurement errors.
s: Equation a1T1 squared = a2T2 squared from the same distance
Ratio 1.5625
Expected ratio 2
Gap is less than expected
Friction and measurement errors as the reason

questions.q:
A cricket coach in Nagpur shows two ways of stopping a ball of 0.16 kg moving at 30 m/s. In the first, the fielder keeps his hands rigid and the ball stops in 0.02 s. In the second, he draws his hands back and the ball stops in 0.10 s. Assume a uniform change of velocity to zero.
(a) Find the acceleration of the ball in each.
(b) Find the force in each.
(c) Which of the two is the way that prevents injury, and why?
(d) Padded gloves also lengthen the stopping time, but a fielder using gloves loses some feel of the ball. Choose between practising the hand-drawing technique and wearing padded gloves for the team, and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) 30/0.02 = 1500 m/s2 and 30/0.10 = 300 m/s2. (b) 0.16 x 1500 = 240 N and 0.16 x 300 = 48 N. (c) The second, since the longer time gives a smaller acceleration and a smaller force. (d) Technique costs practice but no equipment; gloves protect at once but cost feel of the ball. Either choice is accepted with the loss named.
s: Part (a): 1500 and 300 m/s2
Part (b): 240 N and 48 N
Part (c): longer time, smaller force
Part (d): a choice with what is given up

questions.q:
A stalled scooter with its load has a mass of 90 kg on a level road in Indore. Its friction is 160 N once it moves. Meera pushes it with a steady 250 N. Her friend can add 70 N to the push.
(a) Find the acceleration with Meera alone.
(b) How far does the scooter move in 4 s from rest?
(c) With the friend's help, find the new acceleration and the time to travel the same distance.
(d) The friend is at the other end of the road and needs a minute to reach it. Choose whether to wait or to start pushing alone and say what the choice costs.
questions.a: (a) Net force 250 - 160 = 90 N, so a = 1 m/s2. (b) s = 1/2 x 1 x 16 = 8 m. (c) Push 320 N, net 160 N, a = 160/90 = 1.78 m/s2; time = square root of (2 x 8/1.78) = 3.0 s. (d) Starting alone avoids a one-minute delay but takes 1 s longer for the same distance; waiting for help saves a second over the distance but costs the minute. Either is accepted with the cost named.
s: Part (a): 1 m/s2
Part (b): 8 m
Part (c): 1.78 m/s2 and 3.0 s
Part (d): a choice with the cost

questions.q: Sitting on a wheeled chair with her feet off the floor, Isha pushes a very heavy table forward with 30 N. What happens, according to the third law?
questions.a: The table pushes back on Isha with an equal force of 30 N in the opposite direction, so her chair rolls backward.
o: The table pushes back with 30 N and her chair rolls back
The table pushes her back with less than 30 N since it is heavy
The table applies no force since it does not move
The table pushes her back with 30 N but her chair stays still

questions.q: A student says, 'When the canoeist pushes the water backward, the water pushes the paddle forward with an equal force, so the two forces cancel and the canoe cannot move.' What is the flaw?
questions.a: The two forces of the pair act on different objects, the water and the paddle, so they do not cancel. The force on the paddle makes the paddle and the canoe move forward.
o: The two forces act on different objects, so they cannot cancel
The forward force on the paddle is smaller than the backward force
The forces do not occur in pairs when water is involved
The forces cancel but the canoe moves because of its weight

questions.q: Seema is walking on a wet polished floor and slips backward. Which statement explains what went wrong?
questions.a: The floor pushes the foot forward only through friction. On a wet polished floor the friction is small, so the foot slips back when it pushes the ground backward.
o: Too little friction to push the foot forward
The floor pushes back with a force larger than her push
Her foot pushes the floor forward, which makes her fall
The weight of her body becomes smaller on wet floors

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a pair of forces described by Newton's third law?
questions.a: The weight of a box and the normal force on it both act on the box, so they are not a third-law pair. The other three are each a pair acting on two different objects.

The force of the Earth on a fruit and the force of the fruit on the Earth
The force of exhaust gas on a rocket and the force of the rocket on the gas

questions.q: A spacecraft far from planets fires its engine so that the exhaust gases go out in the direction of its motion. What does this do to the spacecraft?
questions.a: The gas is pushed forward, so the gas pushes the spacecraft backward with an equal force, opposite to its motion, and the spacecraft slows down.

It speeds up, since the gas pushes it forward

It speeds up, since the gas leaves ahead of it

questions.q:
Read the statements about Newton's third law.
Statement 1: The two forces of a pair act on the same object and balance each other.
Statement 2: The law applies to magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces as well as to contact forces.
Statement 3: The two forces of a pair are equal in magnitude, but they may produce different accelerations.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the two forces of a pair act on two different objects and do not balance.
o: 2 and 3 only
3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The force with which the Earth pulls a falling fruit is larger than the force with which the fruit pulls the Earth.
Reason (R): The mass of the Earth is much larger than the mass of the fruit.
questions.a: A is false: the two forces are equal and opposite. R is a true statement, but it explains the unequal accelerations, not unequal forces.
o: A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q:
Two skaters, A of mass 60 kg and B of mass 40 kg, stand on smooth ice. A pushes B with 120 N. Match each quantity (column I) with its value (column II).
Column I: 1. Magnitude of the force of B on A  2. Acceleration of A  3. Acceleration of B  4. Direction of the acceleration of B compared with that of A
Column II: a. 2 m/s2  b. 3 m/s2  c. 120 N  d. Opposite
questions.a: By the third law B pushes A with 120 N. Then a = F/m gives 120/60 = 2 m/s2 for A and 120/40 = 3 m/s2 for B, and the two accelerations are in opposite directions.

questions.q: True or False: 'In a push between a light and a heavy skater, the forces on the two are equal, yet the lighter skater gains the larger acceleration.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. By the third law the forces are equal in magnitude, and with a = F/m the object with the smaller mass has the larger acceleration.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: equal forces, and acceleration is inversely proportional to mass

questions.q:
A bullet of 0.02 kg is fired from a gun of 4 kg with a force of 6 N.
(a) What is the recoil force on the gun?
(b) Find the initial accelerations of the bullet and of the gun.
questions.a: (a) By the third law the recoil force on the gun is also 6 N. (b) Bullet: 6/0.02 = 300 m/s2; gun: 6/4 = 1.5 m/s2.
s: Part (a): 6 N on the gun
Part (b): 300 m/s2 and 1.5 m/s2

questions.q:
A fruit of mass 0.2 kg falls near the Earth's surface (g = 9.8 m/s2).
(a) What is the force that the fruit exerts on the Earth?
(b) Why does the Earth not seem to move towards the fruit?
questions.a: (a) The Earth pulls the fruit with 0.2 x 9.8 = 1.96 N, so the fruit pulls the Earth with 1.96 N. (b) The mass of the Earth is so large that its acceleration F/m is far too small to notice.
s: Part (a): 1.96 N
Part (b): huge mass, tiny acceleration

questions.q: Explain with the third law how a rocket lifts off the launch pad.
questions.a: The engine expels gas downward, so the gas pushes the rocket upward with an equal force. When this force is larger than the rocket's weight, the net force is upward and the rocket lifts off.
s: Gas pushed down, equal and opposite force on the rocket upward
Upward force larger than weight gives upward net force

questions.q: What force moves a person forward as she walks, and why are grooves made on the soles of footwear?
questions.a: The foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the foot forward through friction. Grooves increase the friction between the sole and the floor, which prevents slipping.
s: Friction from the ground acts forward on the person
Grooves increase friction to prevent slipping

questions.q: Differentiate between the two forces of a third-law pair and two balanced forces on an object in terms of the objects they act on and whether they cancel.
questions.a: The two forces of a third-law pair act on two different objects, so they do not cancel. Two balanced forces act on the same object and cancel, giving a zero net force.
s: Third-law pair: on different objects, no cancelling
Balanced forces: on the same object, cancel

questions.q: Sana says, 'The canoeist's paddle pushes water backward and the water pushes the paddle forward with equal force, so the canoe cannot move since the forces cancel.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The forces are equal in magnitude but act on different objects, the water and the paddle, so they do not cancel. The forward force on the paddle moves the paddle and the canoe, and a harder push on the water gives a larger forward force.
s: Verdict: not correct
Forces act on different objects
Forward force on the paddle moves the canoe

questions.q: Imran says, 'Newton's third law applies to a man pushing a box but not to two bar magnets pulling each other without touching.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. The third law applies to all kinds of forces, contact or non-contact. Two bar magnets exert equal and opposite magnetic forces on each other, as two charged balloons do with electrostatic forces.
s: Verdict: not correct
Law holds for contact and non-contact forces
Example of magnets or charged balloons

questions.q: Tina says, 'When I push a wall with 50 N, the wall pushes me back with 50 N, so we both accelerate equally.' Is she correct? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The wall does push her back with 50 N, an equal and opposite force. But equal forces do not give equal accelerations: a = F/m differs because the masses are different.
s: Verdict: partly right
First part correct, 50 N back
Second part corrected using a = F/m with different masses

questions.q: For the following, state the action force, its reaction and the effect: (a) a person climbing a coconut tree, (b) a canoeist paddling, (c) a balloon released with its neck open. Say also why a smooth trunk is harder to climb.
questions.a: (a) The legs push down on the trunk; friction from the trunk pushes the person upward. (b) The paddle pushes water backward; the water pushes the paddle and canoe forward. (c) The balloon pushes air out; the air pushes the balloon the opposite way. A smooth trunk gives less friction, so the upward push is smaller and climbing is harder.
s: Climbing: push down, friction pushes up
Paddling: water pushes paddle forward
Balloon: air pushes balloon the opposite way
Each with the effect stated
Smooth trunk, less friction, harder climb

questions.q: Two skaters A (60 kg) and B (40 kg) stand on smooth ice, and A pushes B with a force of 120 N for 0.5 s. Find the force on A, the accelerations of both, their velocities at the end of 0.5 s and the direction of A's motion compared with that of B.
questions.a: Force on A is 120 N opposite to A's push. Accelerations: A = 120/60 = 2 m/s2, B = 120/40 = 3 m/s2. Velocities after 0.5 s from rest: A = 1.0 m/s and B = 1.5 m/s. They move in opposite directions.
s: Force on A is 120 N in the opposite direction
Acceleration of A is 2 m/s2
Acceleration of B is 3 m/s2
Velocities 1.0 m/s and 1.5 m/s
Opposite directions

questions.q:
For the science fair at Bengaluru, a team builds a model rocket of mass 0.8 kg. Its engine expels gas downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward with a steady 14 N. Take g = 9.8 m/s2.
(a) What force does the rocket exert on the gas, and in which direction?
(b) What is the net force on the rocket and its acceleration at lift-off?
(c) If the thrust fell to 7 N, would the rocket lift off?
(d) The team can add a 0.2 kg camera, making the mass 1.0 kg with the same 14 N thrust. Choose whether to add it and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) 14 N downward on the gas. (b) Weight = 0.8 x 9.8 = 7.84 N, so the net force is 14 - 7.84 = 6.16 N upward and a = 6.16/0.8 = 7.7 m/s2. (c) No: 7 N is less than the weight 7.84 N, so the net force is downward. (d) With the camera the weight is 9.8 N, net force 4.2 N and a = 4.2 m/s2: the team gains pictures but loses acceleration. Either choice is accepted with the cost named.
s: Part (a): 14 N downward on the gas
Part (b): net force 6.16 N and 7.7 m/s2
Part (c): 7 N is less than the weight, no lift-off
Part (d): a choice with what is given up

questions.q:
In a classroom activity at a school in Madurai, Pooja (with her chair a total of 40 kg) sits on a chair with smooth wheels facing a trolley-table of 60 kg that also has smooth wheels. She pushes the table with 30 N for 2 s. Ignore friction.

questions.a: (a) 30 N, opposite to her push. (b) Pooja 30/40 = 0.75 m/s2; table 30/60 = 0.5 m/s2. (c) Pooja 1/2 x 0.75 x 4 = 1.5 m; table 1/2 x 0.5 x 4 = 1.0 m. (d) The trolley-table shows both objects moving in opposite directions, which makes the equal and opposite pair visible; the fixed table is simpler but the audience may think the table applies no force. s: Part (a): 30 N in the opposite direction
Part (b): 0.75 and 0.5 m/s2
Part (c): 1.5 m and 1.0 m
Part (d): a choice with what is lost

questions.q: Two boxes of 4 kg and 6 kg joined by a string lie on a frictionless table, and a horizontal force of 30 N pulls the first one. What is the acceleration of the system?

5 m/s2

Read the statements about the two-box system.
Statement 1: The system of two boxes and the string accelerates like a single object of mass m1 + m2.

s: Verdict: false

questions.q:
Two boxes of 6 kg and 4 kg are joined by a string and the first is pulled with 50 N on a frictionless floor.

Only the external force is used

Two boxes of 2 kg and 3 kg stand on a frictionless floor and are pulled by a horizontal force (g = 9.8 m/s2).

Part (b): 49 N, balanced with the weight

questions.q: Explain how the tension on Box 1 and the tension on Box 2 are related by the third law.
questions.a: Box 1 pulls Box 2 through the string with a force T. Box 2 then pulls Box 1 with an equal force T in the opposite direction, so the two tensions are a third-law pair acting on two different boxes.

Opposite in direction on different objects (third-law pair)

questions.a: The internal tension need not be considered, so one equation with the external force and the total mass is enough. The result is the same as the individual analysis.

Result is the same

Right expression F/(m1 + m2)

s: Total mass 8 kg
Force needed 32 N
Acceleration with 24 N is 3 m/s2

questions.q: Two boxes of 3 kg and 5 kg are joined by a string on a frictionless surface and a force of 16 N pulls the first. Find the acceleration of the system, the velocity after 5 s from rest and the distance covered in that time. State which force is internal and which external.

questions.a: a = 30/10 = 3 m/s2. Combined weight = 10 x 9.8 = 98 N downward and the combined normal force is 98 N upward. The system approach is easier since the tension is internal and need not be found, and it gives the same result as the individual analysis.

questions.q:
In a lab at a school in Pune two gliders of 1.5 kg and 2.5 kg are joined by a thread on a frictionless air track. The thread attached to the first glider passes over a pulley and a hanging load pulls it with a steady 3.0 N. The track is 6 m long.

(b) Find the velocity after 4 s and the distance covered in that time.

questions.a: (a) 3.0/(1.5 + 2.5) = 0.75 m/s2. (b) v = 0.75 x 4 = 3 m/s and s = 1/2 x 0.75 x 16 = 6 m. (c) 3.0/5.0 = 0.6 m/s2. (d) Doubling the pull gives a = 6/4 = 1.5 m/s2 and t = 2.83 s; removing the glider gives a = 3/2.5 = 1.2 m/s2 and t = 3.16 s. The first is faster but a heavier load may strain the thread; the second is simpler but is no longer a two-object system. Either choice is accepted with the cost named.
s: Part (a): 0.75 m/s2
Part (b): 3 m/s and 6 m
Part (c): 0.6 m/s2
Part (d): times compared and a choice with its cost

questions.q:

questions.a: (a) 50/100 = 0.5 m/s2. (b) t = 2/0.5 = 4 s. (c) The mass is 120 kg and the force 60 N, so a = 0.5 m/s2. (d) The acceleration is the same, 0.5 m/s2, either way. Carrying the bag with the friend's help moves more load but needs two people; leaving it lets the child manage alone but the bag must travel separately. Either choice is accepted with the cost named.
s: Part (a): 0.5 m/s2
Part (b): 4 s
Part (c): 0.5 m/s2
